description:
Design a 3D-printable handheld gripper (CAD agent task).

Jake (voice, verbatim; first words garbled by transcription — possibly "have a CAD agent work on"): "Can you have a [CAD agent] work on a Helping Hands 3D model? The gripper should be something that I can easily get — thumb on one side, four fingers into the other side of the gripper — so that it easily follows the contours of my hand, and I can squeeze it open and close it."

Spec:
- Parametric CAD source (OpenSCAD, CadQuery or similar) plus STL export, 3D-printable.
- Thumb goes into a pocket on one jaw; the four fingers go into a contoured slot on the opposite jaw, shaped to follow the hand.
- Squeezing closes the jaws, relaxing opens them (spring return, or a hinge/parallel linkage — propose the mechanism).
- Comfortable, parametric for hand size.
- Likely use: handheld demonstration-capture gripper (UMI-style) whose jaws match the robot gripper; include camera mounting points if that fits the project.
- Put renders/screenshots in the pebble reply so Jake can see the design.

results.identified_issue:
Research: generalist.ai text gives no geometry. Sources actually used: (1) photo in x.com/DominiqueCAPaul/status/2040765175779778585 (Apr 2026), fetched via api.fxtwitter.com + images.weserv.nl proxy because pbs.twimg.com doesn't resolve in the sandbox: a collector wearing two devices shows a black cylindrical bar on the back of the hand, a hub under its front end, two black rigid links with a strap/loop around index+middle (front) and thumb (rear), yellow lattice curved tips, a strap round the hand; (2) generalistai.com/assets/pages/blog/gen-1/assets/generalist-gen0-box-folding-handheld-1x.mp4 and generalist-gen1-box-folding-handheld-1x.mp4 frames: the robot-side twin with the same bar, a hub with an AprilTag-style fiducial, and the yellow lattice fingers. Their camera position, sensors and synchronisation mechanism were NOT visible; the gear sync, side camera clip and dovetail are my choices.

Design (cad/openscad/hand_gripper/hand_gripper.scad replaced wholesale; the old sleeve/thumb-cup design is in git history at cb870b8): frame X along the forearm, Z up, Y thumb side. Pivots at (±10,0,0), axis Y; links 10 mm thick in plane y=0 between hub cheeks; the jaws open along X (front-back), like a pinch with the palm down. Gear sectors: module 1.25, pitch r 10, straight-flank trapezoid teeth, thumb gear offset half a tooth. Stop tabs R14/r2.5 at phi = open_max + acos((10-2.5)/14) meet at 22 deg/jaw = 96 mm gape. The digit loops sit at x=±22, y beside the link (index/middle stadium, thumb circle), so a finger at z=-55 is ~25 mm below the pivot height and the fingers slide in the loops as the jaws swing (the pivot isn't on the MCP axis). The camera clip is a C-clip on the Ø22 bar with an arm to y=+62 and a 32 mm UVC plate aimed at (0,0,-110).

build.sh checks: front/thumb bodies (no teeth) vs each other and vs hub empty at 0-21.5 deg for S/M/L; tabs collide at 23; full links with teeth clear at 0-21.5 and jam at 3 deg skew (backlash <3 deg, measured to clear at 1.5 deg skew at 20 deg).

App: Scripts/stage_cad_models.py attaches export/parts.json (file/name/color/explode) to the design as "parts" with model ids. CADDesign.parts ([CADPart]). DesignPage: if parts are non-empty, load every mesh and build an AssemblyScene (a class that keeps the SCNScene and camera stable across SwiftUI updates, explode via an SCNTransaction 0.6 s); the viewport opens exploded, the overlay has an Assemble/Explode capsule and reset; the part picker is replaced by a legend that NavigationLinks to ModelDetailView for each STL. STLs are exported in assembled pose, so the slicer must lay them flat. Typechecked iOS 17 sim + macOS 14 (the 15 non-PebblesKit files); AssemblyScene was rendered headlessly on macOS via SCNRenderer (images in the pebble folder). Not run on device, not built. Other designs remain swipeable. If 'simplify to a single design' meant hiding the other 5 designs from the app, that's not done.
results.summary: Rebuilt the Helping Hands gripper as Generalist's human gripper: seven separate pieces shown in one 3D view that opens pulled apart, with an Assemble button.
results.detailed_description:
I copied Generalist's human gripper from a photo of someone wearing two, plus their robot "handheld" box-folding videos. It has a black bar strapped along the back of your hand and a hub under its front end. Two rigid links hang from the hub, with index + middle in a loop on the front link and your thumb in a loop on the rear one, and yellow lattice tips on the ends. Pinch closes it and spreading opens it, so there's no spring. Gear teeth on the two links make the jaws mirror each other, and stop tabs cap the gape at 96 mm.

The design is seven separate prints: spine, hub, finger link, thumb link, two TPU tips, and a camera clip. They join with a dovetail, M3 pins and a snap clip. Pull the hub off the spine and it still works as a plain hand pincer. In the app it's one design in one 3D view that opens pulled apart. Tap Assemble and the pieces slide together. Under the view, each piece is listed in its colour.

Generalist doesn't show its camera, sensors or how its jaws stay in sync, so the side camera clip and the gears are my own choices. The build checks show nothing collides at any hand size. It hasn't been printed or run on your phone yet. Print the hub, both links and the tips first, and try the pinch.

results.notes:
Jake (voice): "Simplify that Helping Hands view to a single [design]. It should be in the same 3D view, but they should be separated into pieces that can be used independently and yet are connected. Similar to how — if you look at Generalist, if you look at how their gripper for human use works — basically just copy that from videos."

Meaning: show the gripper as ONE design in a single 3D view, as an assembly of separate parts (exploded/assembled toggle) where each part can be printed and used on its own but they connect together. Model the design on Generalist AI's handheld data-collection gripper for humans ("data hands"): research their public videos, images and posts to understand its geometry, how the hand drives the jaws, how the parts split, and camera/sensor mounting, then reproduce that design approach. Relates to the design-viewer pebble voice-965bab93 (app opens straight to the newest design). Don't stop at text sources.

Reference sources (filer's quick pass): text coverage only says Generalist ships thousands of wearable pincer-style "data hands" / grippers — a dummy version of their robot hand that people wear like gloves and puppeteer while doing tasks, capturing micro-movements plus video (500k+ hours). No public text found describing geometry, actuation or camera mounting, so pull those from their videos/images (generalist.ai blog posts, their YouTube and X accounts). Closest documented analog: ETH Zurich hand-held hand-actuated parallel gripper paper.

results.identified_issue:
New part, cad/openscad/hand_gripper/hand_gripper.scad (OpenSCAD 2025.11, matches the repo's existing openscad/crow conventions: build.sh regenerates export/ + render/, STLs force-committed via export/.gitignore '!*.stl').

Mechanism choice: single-pivot angular jaw (not parallel linkage) because it mirrors SO-101 topology (fixed jaw + one rotating jaw) and is two printed parts + one bolt. Fixed jaw = finger sleeve (palm down, fingers straight), moving jaw = thumb cup below. Pivot axis along Y outboard of index finger at the knuckle line (x=-6, z on the jaw contact plane so the closed faces meet flat). Return = rubber band between tail posts behind the pivot (band pulls tails together -> front opens); open stop is a pin on the upper ear placed analytically (a_stop formula) and VERIFIED by build.sh: swing=29 must clash, 0.1-27 deg must not, for S/M/L. Tip radius 126 mm vs SO-101 ~84 mm, so angle->gape mapping differs; recommend recording gape (UMI-style pad visibility) rather than angle.

Assumptions / unverified: hand dims are generic M (finger d 19/19.5/18.5/16.5, lengths 70/78/73/58, thumb d 23), not Jake's measurements. Thumb path from cup rear back to the thenar region passes near the pivot ears - ghost hand in renders suggests clearance but nobody has worn it. Fingers modelled straight (no curl). Camera wedge position (cam_x=22) is a placeholder; no specific camera chosen (plans/handheld_gripper.md prefers USB UVC wide-FOV + iPhone ARKit clip - no phone clip modelled here). Band preload untested. No encoder for jaw angle; an AS5600 magnet at the pivot was considered and skipped to keep a plain through-bolt. Print orientations in README are advice, not sliced. Did not touch plans/handheld_gripper.md or hand_1_0.md; this is a separate purely-mechanical squeeze gripper vs Hand 1.0's servo-trigger design.
results.summary: Modelled a wearable Helping Hands gripper in OpenSCAD: four fingers in a contoured sleeve jaw, thumb in a cup jaw, pinch to close, rubber band springs it open.
results.detailed_description:
Your four fingers lie flat in a sleeve that is the fixed upper jaw. It has one channel per finger with low ridges between them, so it follows your hand. Your thumb sits in a cup underneath, like a sock puppet's mouth. The cup is the lower jaw and swings on one M4 bolt beside your index knuckle. Pinch to close. A rubber band behind the pivot springs it open to a hard stop at 61 mm of gape.

It has the same layout as the SO-101 gripper: one fixed jaw and one pivoting jaw. The tips have TPU pads and a camera wedge on the back of your hand aims at them (1/4"-20 nut plus two M3 holes). There are S/M/L presets and a left-hand mirror, and every hand measurement is a number at the top of the file. build.sh exports the STLs and checks that the jaws never collide at any size and that the stop really catches.

It's untested on a real hand and the hand dimensions are generic. Print lower.stl (the thumb cup) first and try it on. The tight spot is where your thumb runs back past the hinge. Everything is in cad/openscad/hand_gripper/.

summary: The Helping Hands gripper view should become one design in a single 3D view, split into separate parts that print and work independently yet connect. Rework it to copy Generalist AI's human-worn data-collection gripper, researching their videos and images for geometry, hand actuation, part split, and camera mounting.
